lessons.title: Receiving and checking materials
lessons.html:
Materials at a grain handling site

A grain site handles many materials besides grain itself: bags and bulk bags, grain protectants and fumigants, spare parts such as bearings and belts, lubricants, fuel, cleaning materials, sampling consumables and packaging. Each has value and many carry risks. Handling and caring for them properly protects people, the product and the business's money.

Receiving deliveries

  1. Check the delivery note against the purchase order: item, specification, quantity and supplier.
  2. Inspect the condition: damaged packaging, leaks, wet or torn bags, crushed boxes, broken seals.
  3. Check expiry or manufacture dates, especially for chemicals, adhesives and food-contact items.
  4. For hazardous materials, confirm that labels are present and that a safety data sheet (SDS) is available.
  5. Count or weigh the goods. Record shortages and damages on the delivery note before signing, and have the driver acknowledge them.
  6. Capture the receipt in the stock system and move items to the correct storage area promptly.

Do not accept

  • Leaking chemical containers or containers without labels.
  • Agricultural remedies that are not registered in South Africa. Registration falls under Act 36 of 1947; the registration number appears on the label.
  • Goods that do not match the order without approval from the person who ordered them.

Identifying hazards

Learn the hazard pictograms on labels: flammable, toxic, corrosive, harmful, environmental hazard and gas under pressure. The SDS gives detailed information on safe handling, storage, PPE, spills and first aid. Supervisors must make sure SDSs are accessible to workers who handle the material.

lessons.title: Moving and handling materials safely
lessons.html:
Plan the move

Many injuries at grain sites happen while moving materials: back strain from lifting 50 kg bags, crushed feet from falling loads, and forklift accidents. Plan every move before it starts.

Manual handling

  • Assess the load: weight, shape, grip and whether it can shift.
  • Use mechanical aids such as trolleys, pallet jacks, forklifts or conveyors wherever possible.
  • For lifting: feet apart, bend the knees, keep the back straight, hold the load close, lift smoothly with the legs and do not twist. Turn by moving your feet.
  • Use two people or a lifting aid for heavy or awkward loads.
  • Rotate workers on repetitive bag handling to reduce fatigue.

Mechanical handling

  • Only trained and authorised operators may drive forklifts or operate cranes and hoists.
  • Check the rated capacity and never overload.
  • Stack pallets squarely and wrap or strap loads that could slide.
  • Keep pedestrians separated from forklift routes.
  • Never lift a person on forks.

Handling hazardous materials

  • Read the label and SDS before handling.
  • Wear the PPE specified, such as chemical-resistant gloves, goggles and a respirator where required.
  • Keep containers closed and upright; carry them in a secondary container or on a spill tray.
  • Never eat, drink or smoke while handling chemicals.
  • Fumigants such as phosphine-generating products may only be handled by trained, registered persons.

Spills

Stop work, warn others, keep people away and refer to the SDS. Contain the spill with absorbent material and prevent it entering drains or soil. Report it to the supervisor. Dispose of contaminated material as hazardous waste. Wash any skin contact immediately with plenty of water and seek medical help as the SDS directs.

lessons.title: Storing materials correctly
lessons.html:
Principles of good storage

Good storage keeps materials in usable condition, prevents accidents and makes stock easy to find and count.

General storage rules

  • Store items in designated, labelled locations.
  • Keep stores dry, clean, ventilated and free of rodents and birds.
  • Stack bags and boxes on pallets, off the floor and away from walls, within safe heights so stacks cannot topple.
  • Keep heavy items on lower shelves.
  • Keep aisles and emergency exits clear.
  • Use first in, first out (FIFO) so older stock is used before it expires.

Segregation

MaterialStorage requirement
Agricultural chemicals and fumigantsLocked, ventilated chemical store with warning signs, away from food, feed and living areas
Fuel and flammablesAway from ignition sources, with fire extinguishers nearby and bunding to contain spills
Food-grade packagingClean area, away from chemicals, oils and dust
Gas cylindersUpright, chained, in a ventilated area

Never store chemicals in the same room as grain, food, animal feed or seed for planting unless the site design specifically provides separate, sealed compartments.

Security

Materials are a target for theft. Control access to stores, keep chemical stores locked and issue materials only against a requisition. Keys to chemical stores should be held by responsible, trained people.

Protecting materials from damage

Protect bags from rain and sun, bearings from moisture and dust, belts from direct sunlight and rubber from oil. Follow manufacturer storage instructions, including temperature limits.

lessons.title: Stock control, waste and records
lessons.html:
Controlling stock

Materials are money. A silo complex can easily hold hundreds of thousands of rand in spares, bags and chemicals. Good stock control prevents both shortages during harvest and wasteful overstocking.

Issuing materials

  1. Issue only against an approved requisition or job card.
  2. Record what was issued, to whom, for which job and the date.
  3. Return unused items to stock and record the return.

Stock counts

Carry out regular counts, including spot checks of high-value or high-risk items such as fumigants. Compare physical counts with records. Investigate differences and report losses. Chemical use records must reconcile with stock: the amount issued should match the amount applied according to application records.

Reorder levels

Set minimum and reorder levels for critical items, such as elevator belt splices, conveyor bearings and bag stock, based on use and supplier lead times. Plan for higher use before and during the intake season.

Waste and disposal

  • Separate general waste, recyclables, scrap metal, used oil and hazardous waste.
  • Triple rinse empty agrochemical containers where the label allows, puncture them so they cannot be reused and send them to an approved collection or disposal service.
  • Do not burn or bury chemical containers or residues.
  • Keep records of hazardous waste disposal.

Records and responsibility

Keep receiving records, issue and return records, stock count results, SDS files and disposal records. As a supervisor, ensure your team is trained in handling, knows where the SDSs are and reports damage, losses and spills promptly.

Key points

  • Check every delivery against the order, inspect condition and record discrepancies before signing.
  • Read labels and SDSs and wear the specified PPE when handling hazardous materials.
  • Use mechanical aids and correct lifting technique to prevent injuries.
  • Segregate chemicals, flammables and food-contact materials and keep chemical stores locked.
  • Issue against requisitions, count stock regularly and dispose of waste correctly.
